text: Hi, it's Michael. Are you at your desk? I need a quick favour handled discreetly, I'm about to walk into a board meeting and can't talk for long.
tell: Executive voice asking for a 'discreet favour' while unreachable is the classic opening of a cloned-voice payment fraud.

text: Hello, this is David from the CFO's office. The chief executive asked me to reach you directly about a confidential acquisition payment that has to go out today.
tell: Bypassing your normal chain via a named intermediary plus 'confidential' and 'today' in the first breath.

text: Good morning, I'm calling from your supplier's accounts team. We've changed banks after an audit, so please update our payment details before you run this week's invoices.
tell: Vendor bank-detail changes requested by phone are the single most common invoice-redirection fraud.

text: This is part of a deal the board approved last night, and the external law firm is handling it. You'll get an email from their partner in a minute with the paperwork.
tell: A 'lawyer' email arriving on cue is a coordinated second channel controlled by the same fraudster.

text: I've been personally authorised by the chief financial officer to act on this. You won't find it in the usual approval system because it's covered by a non-disclosure agreement.
tell: Explaining away why the payment is missing from the approval system is itself the red flag.

text: I can send you a letter on our company letterhead confirming the new account, signed by our finance director. Our old account is frozen while the audit is going on.
tell: Letterhead is easy to forge; bank changes must be confirmed by calling the vendor on a number already on file.

text: Don't loop in anyone else on the finance team for now, not even your manager. If word of this acquisition gets out before the announcement, the whole deal collapses.
tell: Instructions to skip your manager and dual control are how the fraud avoids the second pair of eyes.

text: Just deal with me directly on this mobile. I'm travelling and my email is unreliable, so don't reply to my work address and please don't call the office.
tell: Blocking the known-good channels (work email, office line) leaves only the channel the attacker controls.

text: Please keep this strictly between the two of us. Treasury will be told after the transfer clears, and I'll take full responsibility if anyone asks you questions.
tell: Pre-emptively absorbing blame lowers the employee's guard against an unapproved transfer.

text: The wire has to reach their account before the bank's cut-off at three o'clock today, or we lose the exclusivity window and the entire deal falls through.
tell: Banking cut-off times are used to rush payments past callback verification.

text: I really need this done in the next twenty minutes. I'm counting on you here, and believe me, this kind of help gets noticed when bonuses are decided.
tell: Reward-and-loyalty pressure from a senior voice replaces process with personal obligation.

text: Our shipment stays on hold until this invoice is settled, and your production line will stop tomorrow if the payment doesn't go out today.
tell: Operational threat from a 'vendor' pressuring payment to details that have not been independently confirmed.

text: Send two hundred and forty thousand dollars to the escrow account details I'm texting you now. Put project consultancy as the reference and send me the confirmation once it's released.
tell: Large wire to new details, vague reference text, confirmation back to the caller: textbook business email compromise payout.

text: Go ahead and buy ten gift cards of five hundred each for the client appreciation event, scratch off the backs and send me photos of the codes.
tell: No business pays anyone with photographed gift card codes; it is untraceable cash-out.

text: Please process the outstanding invoices to the new account number and sort code I've just emailed, and cancel the payment you scheduled to the old details.
tell: Redirecting already-scheduled payments to new details is the moment money is lost; call back on the known number first.
